output: Archive member names, ownership, sizes, timestamps, and object-format headings.
explanation: These describe members of the archive, not functions. Deterministic archives may use zero timestamps.

output: A format name, architecture, BFD flags, and start address.
explanation: Identify the object kind first. A relocatable object normally has no runnable entry point.

output: ELF program-header and dynamic-linking details when present.
explanation: Read LOAD entries as segment mappings. A relocatable .o has no executable program-header layout.

output: An unsupported-option diagnostic or no applicable format-specific information for ELF.
explanation: This format-specific facility is not implemented for ELF; -p is the useful ELF choice. Other object formats define their own OPT values.

output: Section names, sizes, VMA, LMA, disk offsets, alignment, and flags.
explanation: Sizes and addresses are hexadecimal. These are sections, not the PT_LOAD segments displayed by readelf -l.

output: A combined metadata report including headers, symbols, and relocations where available.
explanation: It combines several inspection modes. It does not mean all disassembly or all DWARF records.

output: Address-labelled hexadecimal bytes with an ASCII column.
explanation: The bytes are data. Four printed bytes are not automatically one integer or one instruction.

output: Uncompressed section bytes when the input section is compressed.
explanation: This changes inspection, not the file on disk. Compression support depends on how Binutils was built.

output: The ordinary symbol table with values, bindings, types, sections, sizes, and names.
explanation: g/F means a global function; O denotes an object. In a relocatable ELF, defined symbol values are relative to their sections.

output: Dynamic symbols, often including visibility/version information.
explanation: This is the dynamic linker's symbol view, not every local symbol. On an ordinary .o, a not-a-dynamic-object diagnostic is expected.

output: Relocation offsets, relocation types, and referenced symbols/addends.
explanation: Offsets identify fields to fix. Add -d to place records beside the affected instructions.

output: Dynamic relocation entries when the object has them.
explanation: These describe runtime-linker fixups, unlike the ordinary relocations of an unlinked .o. Use readelf for RELR data.

output: Instructions from sections identified as code.
explanation: Use this first. Symbol boundaries and section classification guide decoding.

output: Disassembly focused on the named symbol.
explanation: Use the exact stored name. For a mangled C++ function, obtain it from -t rather than guessing its demangled spelling.

output: A best-effort instruction decoding of the selected data section.
explanation: Valid-looking instructions do not prove the bytes are code. -D also changes how symbol boundaries constrain decoding.

output: Only the named sections appear in the selected output mode.
explanation: Repeat -j to keep more than one section. Combine it with an action such as -s, -d, or -h.

output: Assembly rendered with the requested target-specific options.
explanation: The options after -M are decoder suboptions, not standalone objdump flags. The x86 options are listed separately below.

output: Raw bytes decoded using the specified machine model.
explanation: Required when raw input has no architecture metadata. The wrong machine can produce plausible but wrong instructions.

output: Input interpreted as the requested BFD object format.
explanation: binary means raw bytes, while elf64-x86-64 means an ELF container. Check supported names with -i.

output: Disassembly using a supported target's big-endian interpretation.
explanation: Replace TARGET with a suitable architecture. This is not a byte-reversal switch and is not meaningful for x86's fixed little-endian instructions.

output: Disassembly using a supported target's little-endian interpretation.
explanation: Useful for formats that omit byte-order metadata. It affects decoding, not stored file bytes.

output: Zero runs are decoded rather than replaced with an ellipsis.
explanation: More output is not necessarily more code; alignment padding and data can contain zero bytes.

output: Instructions at or above the chosen address.
explanation: Addresses are in the object's disassembly coordinate, not disk byte offsets. In our .text fixture, main starts at 0x14.

output: Instructions before the exclusive stop address.
explanation: The pair [0,0x14) selects the fixture's add function. Prefer a symbol filter when addresses are not known.

output: Displayed addresses shifted by OFFSET.
explanation: A reporting adjustment does not relocate a running program, apply link fixups, or modify the ELF.

output: Extra file-offset annotations at displayed regions/symbols.
explanation: The annotation connects disassembly to original disk bytes; it is not an offset column on every instruction line.

output: A listing with address fields suppressed.
explanation: Useful for comparing instruction text across builds; it removes context rather than changing decoding.

output: A full address-style prefix on instruction lines.
explanation: This older listing style changes layout. It normally suppresses raw bytes unless --show-raw-insn is added.

output: Instruction encodings appear alongside the assembly.
explanation: Bytes such as 55 are machine encodings; they are not separate source statements.

output: Assembly without the machine-byte column.
explanation: Useful for a compact reading view. Keep bytes when diagnosing instruction length or an encoding problem.

output: A raw-byte field sized for WIDTH bytes per output line.
explanation: This controls wrapping; it does not force the CPU instruction length to WIDTH.

output: All symbol labels sharing a displayed address.
explanation: Aliases can name the same location. Multiple labels do not imply multiple instruction copies.

output: Target-special symbols are included if available.
explanation: Some targets use mapping or marker symbols. The simple x86 fixture may not show an additional special symbol.

output: C++ encodings become names such as add(int, int).
explanation: Name presentation changes; the machine code and symbol addresses stay the same. STYLE selects a supported naming convention.

output: Demangling with the recursion guard enabled.
explanation: Normal output is unchanged; the guard limits pathological nested symbol decoding.

output: Demangling without that recursion-depth guard.
explanation: Relevant only to extremely nested names. It can exhaust stack resources, so keep the default for ordinary inspection.

output: Wide fields are less likely to wrap or truncate.
explanation: Helpful when symbol names or section rows exceed a traditional terminal width.

output: Non-ASCII names are displayed according to METHOD.
explanation: Methods are default, locale, invalid, hex, escape, and highlight; the effect concerns text display, not machine-code decoding.

output: With visualization enabled, local branch arcs appear beside instructions.
explanation: Modes are the bare option, color, extended-color, or off. Straight-line add has no branch arcs to draw.

output: Instruction text gains or loses terminal color sequences.
explanation: Modes include off, terminal, on/color/colour, and extended/extended-color/extended-colour. This does not add semantic execution information.

output: Source statements mixed into the disassembly when debug mappings and source are available.
explanation: Implies -d. Missing source lines do not prove missing machine code; the reference fixture intentionally has no DWARF.

output: Interleaved source lines receive the chosen prefix.
explanation: This distinguishes C text from instructions; with no TEXT, the usual marker is a hash followed by a space.

output: File and line labels near disassembly or relocation entries.
explanation: Requires suitable debug information and a relevant action such as -d or -r.

output: Inline call-site chains are shown when recorded in the debug data.
explanation: At -O0 the tiny program may have no inlined frames; optimized code can map one address to several source contexts.

output: The first displayed source context can extend to the start of that file.
explanation: It changes the amount of source shown, not which instructions execute.

output: Source lookup also searches DIR.
explanation: This helps objdump find files while rendering output; it does not add a compiler include path to a build.

output: Recorded absolute source paths are remapped under PREFIX.
explanation: Useful when a binary was built elsewhere. It does not edit the paths stored in the ELF.

output: Initial components are stripped before adding the source prefix.
explanation: Only meaningful with --prefix. Use it to match the current source-tree layout.

output: Available DWARF sections are decoded into records.
explanation: Potentially a very large report. Choose one subtype below when you only need line numbers or unwind rules.

output: Abbreviation entries listing DWARF tags and attribute forms.
explanation: These are templates used to decode debug entries, not the values of your C variables.

output: Entries from the DWARF address table.
explanation: Other debug records can reference these indexed addresses. No table means no matching output.

output: Address ranges associated with compilation units.
explanation: Use the ranges to identify which compilation unit describes a code address.

output: Compilation-unit or type-unit index contents.
explanation: Mainly useful with indexed or split debug packages; a basic object may have no index.

output: Decoded file/line/address associations.
explanation: Read each row as a source location associated with a code address. Optimized mappings can be many-to-many.

output: Line-table headers and line-program operations.
explanation: This is the encoding behind decodedline, not assembly instructions executed by the CPU.

output: Raw frame-description and call-frame instruction records.
explanation: These describe how to recover caller state; they are not a live process stack trace.

output: Unwind rules rendered in a more tabular interpreted form.
explanation: Track the canonical frame address and saved-register rules across instruction ranges.

output: Debug-name or GDB index data when present.
explanation: An index speeds symbol/debug lookup; it is not the function's machine code.

output: Debug Information Entries with tags, attributes, names, and offsets.
explanation: DW_TAG_subprogram describes a function; DW_AT_name names it. Offset fields locate metadata records, not necessarily machine instructions.

output: Location lists describing where variables can be found over address ranges.
explanation: A variable can move between registers and memory or be unavailable in optimized code.

output: Macro definitions and macro-import records when emitted.
explanation: Build with suitable macro debug information, such as GCC -g3; ordinary -g need not record all macros.

output: Public-name index entries when present.
explanation: These help map names to debug records. They are not the same table as objdump -T.

output: Public-type index entries when present.
explanation: Entries point to type metadata; newer compiler configurations may omit these indexes.

output: DWARF range-list records.
explanation: The uppercase R matters. A function can occupy several disjoint ranges after optimization.

output: String-bearing debug sections and their offsets.
explanation: Offsets select strings referenced by other DWARF records, not runtime C string addresses.

output: The string-offset table used by indexed debug forms.
explanation: An entry is an indexable offset into debug strings, not a pointer to the target process.

output: Abbreviation data from trace-related debug sections if present.
explanation: This is specialized metadata. An ordinary GCC object often contains none.

output: Trace-related address-range metadata if present.
explanation: Do not interpret absence as a missing function or a failed disassembly.

output: Trace-related debug records when present.
explanation: It is not a recording of instructions executed by your program.

output: References to separate debug files and related link metadata.
explanation: A debuglink names another metadata file; it is not a function call or an ELF shared-library dependency.

output: Requested debug data can also come from linked debug files.
explanation: Defaults depend on the build. When network debug lookup is enabled, this may consult configured debuginfod services.

output: Only local requested debug data is used, without following debug-file links.
explanation: Useful when you want a self-contained view of the input's own metadata.

output: Missing separate debug information may be fetched through configured debuginfod services.
explanation: Conditional on build support and server configuration. This enables lookup; it does not create debug information.

output: Debug inspection proceeds without debuginfod network lookup.
explanation: Build support and option availability vary; this is distinct from disabling all local debug links.

output: Deeply nested debug entries are omitted.
explanation: Depth zero means no depth limit. This changes metadata verbosity, not machine-code recursion.

output: The debug-entry dump begins at the selected offset.
explanation: Use an actual entry offset from the debug report. An arbitrary byte inside an entry is not a meaningful starting point.

output: Additional consistency diagnostics may accompany the debug dump.
explanation: No diagnostic is not a proof that every byte of the ELF is valid.

output: Separate debug-file lookup additionally searches DIR.
explanation: This locates debug metadata files, unlike -I, which searches source-text paths.

output: Global-variable location/type information derived from supported DWARF records.
explanation: Requires suitable debug entries. The reference fixture contains symbols but no DWARF, so it has no such variable map.

output: Selected non-debug information from linked separate debug files can also be processed.
explanation: Implies following debug links. It is not a request to print every section from every library dependency.

output: Debug information decoded through the supported legacy debugging path.
explanation: For a DWARF-focused task, prefer an explicit --dwarf subtype. Results depend on debug format and build support.

output: Supported debug information is formatted in a tags-oriented style.
explanation: A specialized legacy/debug view; it does not promise C source reconstruction.

output: STABS debug-section records if the file has them.
explanation: Modern Linux builds usually use DWARF, so no STABS output is normal.

output: Compact C Type Format type dictionaries from the selected section, usually .ctf.
explanation: Type records describe types, not instructions. Requires CTF-bearing input and corresponding tool support.

output: CTF child dictionaries are resolved using the named parent archive member.
explanation: Useful for CTF archives with a nondefault parent; not a general ELF parent-process option.

output: The CTF parent dictionary is read from another section.
explanation: A specialized documented option for unusual CTF layouts; availability can vary with version.

output: SFrame unwind metadata from the selected section, normally .sframe.
explanation: Needs SFrame data and tool support. Like DWARF frame records, it is unwind metadata rather than a live backtrace.

output: Supported object-format and machine names plus compatibility information.
explanation: Use these exact names with -b and -m. A host tool does not necessarily support every target architecture.

output: Tool identity, version, build annotation, and license text.
explanation: Record the version with a reproducible report. A development snapshot may include a date after the release number.

output: The options and target-specific decoder settings supported by this build.
explanation: This is the final authority for flags available on your installed executable.

output: Options are loaded from the response file before normal inspection.
explanation: Put options such as -d and -M intel in options.txt. The response file is not a shell script.

output: Intel-style operands such as mov rbp,rsp.
explanation: Destination comes first. This does not change the instruction bytes.

output: AT&T-style operands such as mov %rsp,%rbp.
explanation: Source comes first; register names have percent prefixes and immediates commonly use a dollar prefix.

output: Bytes are decoded in 64-bit x86 mode.
explanation: A raw-byte mode selection, not proof that the input really contains x86-64 code.

output: Bytes are decoded in 32-bit x86 mode.
explanation: Using it on a 64-bit byte stream can change instruction boundaries and register interpretation.

output: Bytes are decoded in 16-bit x86 mode.
explanation: Select it for an appropriate raw code image, not as a way to convert a 64-bit ELF into a 16-bit program.

output: Intel-oriented mnemonic naming is selected.
explanation: This suboption can also imply Intel syntax; use -M intel for the usual beginner-friendly setting.

output: AT&T-oriented mnemonic naming is selected.
explanation: This is a mnemonic/syntax presentation choice rather than another instruction set.

output: A 64-bit default address-size interpretation is requested.
explanation: Mode options and encoded prefixes can override defaults. It does not resize the input file's addresses.

output: A 32-bit default address-size interpretation is requested.
explanation: For specialist raw decoding; choose the real execution mode rather than using it to make a listing look smaller.

output: A 16-bit default address-size interpretation is requested.
explanation: Address size concerns effective-address calculation, distinct from the operand's data width.

output: A 32-bit default operand-size interpretation is requested.
explanation: A default does not erase explicit size prefixes or the effects of the selected execution mode.

output: A 16-bit default operand-size interpretation is requested.
explanation: Use for the relevant raw-code context. It is not a conversion of 32-bit variables into 16-bit values.

output: Mnemonic size suffixes are printed more explicitly when supported.
explanation: For example a suffix can distinguish byte, word, long, and quadword forms; support varies with syntax.

output: The AMD64 ISA interpretation is selected for relevant encodings.
explanation: An ISA-selection aid, not a performance analyzer for AMD processors.

output: The Intel64 ISA interpretation is selected for relevant encodings.
explanation: Most ordinary instructions look the same; some overlapping encodings depend on the selected ISA.

output: Immediate values can gain matching symbol annotations.
explanation: Useful for linked executables/shared objects; the relocatable fixture is not the intended input for this feature.
